data.title: China Fears New Export Curbs on Chips After Nvidia Scandal
data.description:
China is worried that the scandal at US tech giant Nvidia – which saw its CEO Jensen Huang resign on Thursday over alleged extramarital affairs and espionage – will lead to tougher export controls on the company’s world-leading computer chips.

Beijing warned the United States on Friday not to impose additional curbs on chip exports.

Asked about calls from US lawmakers to impose more limits on chip equipment, foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a regular briefing that China “has consistently opposed the abuse of export control measures, which disrupts the stability of global industrial and supply chains and serves no party’s interests.”

 

ALSO SEE: Huang Resigns as Head of Nvidia, Kress Made Interim CEO

 

“China and the United States should work together to implement the important consensus reached by their respective heads of state and maintain the stable development of China-US economic and trade relations,” Mao said.

It’s been like that all week. On Thursday, Beijing accused the US of using spurious spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological “blockade” on China.

“China’s technological progress is driven by independent innovation and open cooperation. The US side should stop fabricating such ‘spy’ narratives as a pretext for imposing a technological blockade,” Mao said.

Jensen Huang, the Nvidia co-founder and global chip titan, stepped down on Thursday after admitting to an affair, reportedly with Alice Huang, a former senior executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.

That was the bombshell news of the week, which has put an intense media focus on both Jensen and Alice, who are not related, but also the Chinese woman’s suspect business dealings.

Reports allege that the Commerce Department under Secretary Howard Lutnick may have failed to act on suspicions that Megaspeed was helping to reroute restricted Nvidia chips to China.

US media quoted US lawmakers as saying they are in favour of imposing additional export controls on chips to China as a result of the snowballing scandal.

“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here. I’m in favour of limiting those exports,” House speaker Mike Johnson was quoted as saying.

“I think there is a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.”

US intelligence reportedly circulated a memo this spring alleging that Alice Huang was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security.

Beijing has rejected the allegations and said on Thursday they were a “pretext for imposing a technological blockade” to stop China advancing in artificial intelligence technology.

The furore comes ahead of a meeting expected next week between US President Donald Trump and Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in Shenzhen in southern China at an APEC gathering.

 

US lawmakers summon Huang

Meanwhile, US lawmakers have called the former Nvidia CEO, who is a key architect of the AI boom, to face questioning in December over his dealings with Alice Huang, who US officials suspect was a Chinese spy.

The scandal has wiped almost half a trillion dollars off Nvidia’s market value, but their affair raised concern on whether Megaspeed, Alice Huang’s data centre firm in Singapore, was used to help Chinese companies such as Alibaba get access to advanced Nvidia chips, via a subsidiary in Malaysia, or directly into China.

“Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology,” Republican Senator Tim Scott wrote Thursday on X.

Scott said he was requesting Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify in December before the Senate Banking Committee, which he chairs.

It joins a call for a closed-door interview with the leather-jacketed, 63-year-old Huang on December 1 by three House of Representatives committees, on threat of subpoena, AFP reported.

US intelligence reportedly circulated a memo in spring this year alleging that Alice Huang was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Beijing has rejected that allegation.

On Wednesday, The New York Times reported a second affair, citing video of Huang being affectionate with Nvidia’s vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell.

Nvidia’s board announced late on Thursday that chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO, while it searches for a permanent successor to Huang, who spent 33 years at the helm of the firm he co-founded.

Nvidia hit gold when the launch of OpenAI’s ChatGPT in 2022 sparked a global rush to develop AI, with its processors – once designed for video game graphics – becoming a crucial ingredient to train and run the technology.

Huang, who was born in Taiwan, was a close informal adviser to President Donald Trump on AI, and had spent years lobbying against curbs on sales of advanced AI chips to China for national security reasons.

Singapore barred Chinese ‘spy’

Singapore said on Thursday it had barred Alice Huang, a Chinese national, from re-entering the country in February for giving investigators inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed, though she was not investigated for espionage.

Nvidia’s board opened a probe on Sunday into reporting that Huang had been the target of a “foreign intelligence effort,” while saying it retained confidence in him.

At the heart of the spy allegations is the race between the United States and China for supremacy in an industry widely seen as the next industrial revolution.

Singapore’s home ministry said it had repeatedly sought information from the US Justice Department and FBI on a US server supplier during its Megaspeed probe, but “received limited information or assistance.”

Malaysia also said on Friday that it was investigating a subsidiary of Megaspeed International over the possible diversion of advanced AI chips to other countries.

Alice Huang’s tangled corporate web

Singapore-based tech group Megaspeed dealt in billions of dollars’ worth of the world’s most advanced AI chips, but its office was an empty shell when AFP visited, its staff seemingly vanished long before claims of espionage landed at their door.

Details about Alice Huang’s life have been revealed by a range of media outlets. AFP said it is hard to pin down where she lives or works currently, but some suspect she is back in China.

Business filings in Singapore described her as a Chinese citizen with a Hong Kong passport.

She was born in China’s landlocked Hunan province, which she left to study media in Hong Kong, HK01 media reported.

Huang, now in her late 40s, did a master’s degree in media management at Hong Kong Baptist University in the late 2000s.

A CCTV reporter wrote on Weibo that she worked with Huang at the Chinese broadcaster, but later deleted the post, AFP reported.

A corporate CV published by a Chinese investment firm details her rapid ascent through the ranks of Asian investment banking.

She served in a senior role at HSBC sometime around 2012, the resume claims, before moving on to stints at CITIC Securities and Shanghai Hexi Investment.

She married Kang Wei, a Chinese businessman, who The Wall Street Journal said had met Jensen Huang through their mutual involvement in video game businesses.

In fact, the Journal said Kang “appeared to accept his wife’s romantic relationship with the Nvidia CEO and spoke openly of their closeness.”

AFP said corporate records filed in Hong Kong show that Alice Huang sits in the middle of a corporate web, connected to myriad shell companies, investment houses and major Chinese technology firms.

They list her as a director of Nanjing Lingxing Technology, which operates the popular T3 ride-hailing platform in China.

Other notable investors in Nanjing Lingxing Technology include Alibaba and Tencent, as well as state-backed carmakers like China FAW and Dongfeng Motor Group.

 

Megaspeed linked to chip deals

Megaspeed touts itself as a company at the heart of the AI revolution, using Nvidia’s advanced silicon chips to power high-performance computing inside vast data centres.

But it is also under investigation for serving a murkier purpose. Under the guise of buying computer hardware for its Southeast Asia data hubs, Megaspeed allegedly helped Beijing skirt trade restrictions by sending Nvidia chips into China.

Beijing has denied allegations of spying, and Megaspeed said it was investigating if it had complied with export controls on the sensitive chips, AFP said.

At Megaspeed’s office in the heart of the Singapore business district, no staff could be seen behind its locked glass doors. Neighbours told AFP they had not seen anyone come or go for the past few months.

Likewise in a mall at a newly developed neighbourhood in Johor, the Malaysian region a bridge away from Singapore, no employees were around in subsidiary Speedmatrix’s office.

Singapore police opened an investigation in February 2025 into Megaspeed and several other companies suspected of circumventing or violating export controls.

Alice Huang was interviewed as part of Singapore’s probe. Although no charges were laid, she was barred from the city-state in February 2026 for providing inaccurate information to “downplay her role in Megaspeed”, Singapore’s home ministry said.

 

Records show huge jump in income

Corporate records show Huang’s direct involvement in the birth of Megaspeed. A company linked to her acquired the Singapore arm of Chinese video game developer 7Road International in early 2023.

Almost immediately, the 7Road name was changed to Megaspeed International. Alice Huang was listed as a Megaspeed director for less than a year, taking the role between March and November 2023.

Her arrival coincided with a drastic change in fortunes, as Megaspeed pivoted from a little-known video game-maker to one of Asia’s biggest buyers of Nvidia chips.

Within 12 months, Megaspeed’s revenue jumped from $0 to almost $300 million, according to company accounts filed in 2024.

Megaspeed – which described itself as a “cloud hosting services provider” – saw the value of its assets skyrocket from $32 million to almost $3 billion over the same period.

Just one of Nvidia’s advanced AI computer chips can cost tens of thousands of dollars. And over two years, Megaspeed reportedly traded in upwards of $4 billion worth of Nvidia chips.

A financial trail weaving through Singapore, Malaysia and the Cayman Islands suggests Megaspeed’s business may have been boosted by a connection to Chinese tech giant Alibaba, AFP said.

Megaspeed has a Malaysian subsidiary that struck a deal in 2024, pledging assets to Apex Enterprise Solutions in Singapore as security in case of contractual breaches.

Apex is linked through a parent company to Alibaba Group Holding Ltd, a firm registered in the Cayman Islands, Singapore corporate data shows.

By that time, Huang was no longer registered as a director at Megaspeed. But Singapore authorities said she remained one of Megaspeed’s “key controllers”.

Megaspeed’s ultimate holding company is a Singapore firm called Swiftdata.

 

Awkward questions

In June 2025, US investigators turned up at Megaspeed to carry out a “post-shipment verification”, with Huang present, according to Singapore’s home ministry, adding that it was the first time it found out about Washington’s probe.

On the same day, Huang was interviewed by Singapore police, who impounded her passport. By then, she and Nvidia boss Jensen Huang had already been spotted together in public.

In one of their early outings together, they were seen mingling at a party after the Computex trade show in Taiwan at the beginning of 2024.

Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings about their relationship well before it exploded into a public scandal, but said Sunday he did not regret not acting on it.

“No, I don’t think so. I think – you know, he’s an honorable guy,” Trump said.

But with China and the United States fighting for supremacy in artificial intelligence, Nvidia’s market-leading products have become a major point of contention.

Nvidia controls an estimated 90% of the market for the chips used to train and run AI models, and the US imposed rules in 2022 to restrict their sales to China.

A Chinese university tied to the nation’s defence establishment was able to buy advanced Nvidia chips, according to procurement notices from October and September.

Singapore’s probe into Megaspeed is ongoing. And Malaysia said on Friday it’s also investigating the company’s subsidiary Speedmatrix to determine if chips imported into the country had been exported to other jurisdictions.

Megaspeed itself said it has retained a US law firm to examine its compliance.

“Megaspeed takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously,” it said.

 

  • Jim Pollard with Agence France-Presse

data.title: Nvidia Board ‘Ponders Ousting Huang’; Indonesian VP Resigns
data.description:
Upheaval at Nvidia – the world’s top chipmaker – intensified on Thursday amid reports the company’s board was meeting to decide whether to oust and replace CEO Jensen Huang.

This followed a New York Times report alleging the company founder had a second extramarital affair, including one with a woman accused of spying for China.

The scandal has sent shares of the multi-trillion dollar behemoth plunging in after-hours trading. The fate of Huang, who has been a key promoter of the artificial intelligence boom, is uncertain, as media around the world also scrutinize his company’s chip dealings with China.

 

ALSO SEE: Global Leaders Heading to Asia for Talks on Trade, AI and Nukes

 

Huang, 63, has spent years lobbying against curbs on sales of advanced AI chips to China, and US President Donald Trump last year cleared Nvidia’s H200 chips for export there over objections from Beijing’s critics in both parties.

The chip giant’s board met on Wednesday to weigh Huang’s future, according to CNN and the New York Times. Nvidia has not made any statements about the outcome of the meeting.

Beijing has rejected the spying allegations and claimed that the US was using spurious claims as a pretext to impose a technological ‘blockage’ on China.

“China’s technological progress is driven by independent innovation and open cooperation. The US side should stop fabricating such ‘spy’ narratives as a pretext for imposing a technological blockade,” foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a regular briefing on Thursday.

Nvidia shares were down around 25% from their all-time high in early October and the scandal has raised questions over who could replace Huang if he is ousted.

The rapidly unfolding story exploded after reports that Huang, who has been married to Lori Huang for over 40 years, was involved in an extramarital romance.

 

The Nvidia CEO has since admitted to having an affair, reportedly with Alice Huang, who was a senior executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.

US intelligence reportedly circulated a memo earlier this year alleging Alice Huang was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security.

Alice Huang was among the attendees at a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang at a Chinese restaurant in Taipei on May 22, 2025, during Computex, the island’s top tech expo.

At one point, Jensen Huang can be seen putting his arm around Alice Huang as she kisses him on the right cheek, press livestreams show, AFP reported.

She visited Taiwan a total of eight times in 2024 and 2025, a Taiwanese government minister said Thursday.

Nvidia’s board had already announced on Sunday a probe of what it called reporting that Jensen Huang had been the target of a “foreign intelligence effort”.

Then came a New York Times report on Wednesday that the Nvidia co-founder was involved in a second extramarital affair, saying there was video evidence of the 63-year-old executive being affectionate with Nvidia’s vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell.

Powell, 48, has been a public face of Nvidia’s efforts to expand the chip technology into higher education and healthcare, and was speaking at a San Jose, California conference where they “were seen being affectionate at the hotel” by bystanders, the Times reported.

The chip giant’s code of conduct tells associates to avoid conflicts of interest, and cites the example of “personal relationships”.

“We avoid situations where our actions might create a conflict – actual or potential – between our personal gain and our obligations to Nvidia”, the code says.

 

Possible ouster

Nvidia’s bylaws require a majority of the 11 board directors to remove Huang as CEO. But he would retain his board seat, which could only be taken away by shareholders.

Several directors want to appoint Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim leader, according to US news outlet Semafor.

An outside firm is helping the board identify potential replacements, Bloomberg News reported.

Huang has repeatedly avoided naming a successor when the question is brought up.

The New York Times earlier reported that the tech CEO has been called on by Congress to provide a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang.

As the artificial intelligence industry surge has spurred Nvidia’s stock prices to new heights, Huang has appeared at US President Donald Trump’s side at White House events, as recently as last month when he accepted a National Medal of Science from the Republican leader.

Huang was among the world’s most influential tech leaders – including Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and Mark Zuckerberg – who vowed to self-regulate AI against possible threats, as Trump rejected calls for government oversight and dismissed warnings the technology could wipe out humanity.

Nvidia shareholders filed a class action lawsuit against Huang and the AI chip maker for failing to disclose information about the relationship to investors.

Founded in 1993, Nvidia designs advanced components originally created to handle 3D visuals in video games, called Graphics Processing Units (GPUs).

Nvidia’s processors are mostly made by Taiwanese company TSMC, the world’s largest contract manufacturer of chips.

Nvidia is scheduled to release its quarterly results on November 17.

 

Indonesian political crisis

Meanwhile, in other Asian news, Indonesia’s vice president resigned Thursday, undone by a scandal over his high school diploma that has added to pressure on a government facing widespread dissatisfaction over the economy, graft and wildfires.

There had been repeated calls for Gibran Rakabuming Raka, 39, to step down following a Supreme Court ruling last month to annul his high school qualification, obtained abroad.

On Thursday, he submitted his resignation to President Prabowo Subianto and to parliament.

Prabowo told reporters he had accepted Gibran’s resignation “with a heavy heart” and praised him for acting “for a greater cause, for the interests of the nation, the state, and the people of Indonesia”.

“He certainly feels that he has pursued his education through an orderly process, but we all understand that the education system abroad is different from the education system in Indonesia,” the president said.

Indonesia’s vice president does not have many constitutionally defined powers apart from acting as the president’s representative at official events and taking over if his boss is incapacitated.

‘Political realignment’

Gibran’s downfall came after thousands of Indonesians took to the streets in recent weeks to protest economic hardship, graft, perceived authoritarianism and the government’s handling of months of devastating wildfires emitting toxic haze.

His exit is likely to complicate a loose governing alliance that includes the parties of Prabowo and of his predecessor Joko Widodo – Gibran’s father, who goes by Jokowi.

The resignation “marks a significant political realignment, but does not necessarily threaten government stability”, according to Khairul Fahmi, executive director of the Institute for Security and Strategic Studies (ISESS) think tank.

“Jokowi will retain political influence, but Gibran’s departure could reduce his network’s direct access to power. For Prabowo, this creates greater room to consolidate his leadership and pursue his own political agenda,” Khairul told AFP.

Two years into his term, Prabowo’s popularity has reached record lows.

Last week, Indonesian authorities arrested the former national police chief and three senior police officials for allegedly tapping the president’s telephone.

On Thursday, police said they were investigating possible treason.

Prabowo’s rise to power was widely credited to support from the popular Jokowi, who served two terms from 2014 to 2024.

The choice of Gibran as running mate strengthened ties between Prabowo’s Gerindra party and figures aligned to Jokowi, until then a political rival who had defeated Prabowo twice in presidential elections.

Under the alliance, Gibran and other Jokowi allies were appointed to key positions in the government of Prabowo, who is seen as close to the military while the police has traditionally been loyal to Jokowi.

Youngest-ever VP

Gibran became the youngest person ever to hold Indonesia’s vice presidency. Then, two years into his term, detractors went to court to challenge his high school certificate – a prerequisite for the job.

Gibran had completed his schooling in Singapore before going on to study for a marketing degree there.

When submitting his candidacy to the General Elections Commission (KPU) in 2024, he filed a certificate stating his overseas education was equivalent to a vocational high school in Indonesia.

Last month, however, Indonesia’s Supreme Court ruled to invalidate the document, prompting moves in parliament to unseat him.

Gibran has consistently defended his credentials. “If I didn’t graduate from high school, then I obviously wouldn’t have been able to go to college. I studied up to a bachelor’s degree in Singapore,” he has said.

Prabowo now has 14 days to submit two names from which parliament will have two months to pick Gibran’s replacement.

Researcher Arya Fernandes of Indonesia’s Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) told AFP Prabowo will likely seek “a candidate who is acceptable to all coalition members to avoid triggering divisions within the coalition” that includes Jokowi’s party.

“The vice-presidential candidate nominated by Prabowo could potentially become his running mate in 2029, or emerge as a political competitor. He will therefore carefully weigh the pros and cons of each potential nominee,” he said.

 

  • AFP with additional input and editing by Jim Pollard

data.title: Global Leaders Heading to Asia for Talks on Trade, AI and Nukes
data.description:
Senior officials from China, the US and Russia have been discussing an international agreement to try to prevent or restrict the use of artificial intelligence in decisions about countries’ nuclear weapons.

The talks come ahead of the APEC summit in Shenzhen next week, where President Xi Jinping is expected to meet Russian leader Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi on Wednesday about a possible trilateral summit with Beijing and Moscow.

 

ALSO SEE: Chinese Exports Soar in October, as Trade Surplus Tops $1 Trillion

 

“They agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation, including at any potential trilateral leaders’ meeting with Russia,” the US State Department said afterward.

Sources told the South China Morning Post that officials from the three countries have been discussing “the agenda and protocol for talks between the countries’ leaders” on the sidelines of the Apec summit on November 18 and 19.

“The sources said that the war in Ukraine and denuclearisation of the Korean peninsula had largely fallen off the table as possible topics,” so the focus shifted “to areas of potential consensus, particularly the role of artificial intelligence in nuclear command and control.”

Trade, AI and nukes – they’re important and hot issues – but analysts aren’t expecting too much in terms of outcomes.

Trump has raised the issue of denuclearisation many times in recent weeks, saying last month that it would be “a very positive thing for the world.”

The US president said on Sunday he thought he would meet Xi and Putin in Shenzhen to discuss ending the war in Iran and denuclearisation.

And last month he said he was open to three-way arms control talks with Xi and Putin, which he said would focus on nuclear weapons, although China has appeared less keen on such discussions.

 

China cool on nukes agreement

The talks sound worthy, but China’s hesitant. Its foreign ministry said in October its “nuclear strength is by no means at the same level with that of the US and Russia” and it would be “neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join the so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage”.

The AI aspect of denuclearisation was raised initially by Ro Khanna, a member of the US House Select Committee on China, just before the summit in Washington between Presidents Trump and Xi in September, when they were expected to discuss issues related to AI.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer have also been discussing economic and AI-related issues with Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng.

China’s commerce ministry said last week that any further agricultural purchases from the US would be tied to the implementation of an agreement to cut reciprocal tariffs on $30 billion worth of products from each side.

Analysts who spoke to AFP said expectations on the likelihood of major outcomes on trade or denuclearisation should be kept to a minimum.

“The symbolism… will account for a good portion of its substance,” the Brookings Institution’s Ryan Hass told AFP.

While he expects Xi and Putin to give Trump “a respectful hearing” on arms control, Hass said they will likely only “agree on broad principles without committing to any follow-on actions”.

Wang Wen, dean of Renmin University’s Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies, agreed major outcomes were unlikely, calling it “a high probability that talks could end without a breakthrough”.

Separately, a meeting Trump once hoped for with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un appears dead in the water, with Pyongyang rejecting repeated overtures, AFP said.

 

AI deal possible

But artificial intelligence will be a hot topic at APEC, after Xi and Trump agreed in September to set up a “communication channel” for AI incidents.

Trump has repeatedly dismissed fears that AI could pose a threat to humanity. But despite the countries’ fierce tech rivalry, calls for cooperation are growing due to shared concerns regarding bioweapons and infrastructure hacking.

Xi said in September that Washington and Beijing have a responsibility to “develop and manage AI for good and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control”.

Bessent is expected to meet He Lifeng next week ahead of Trump’s meeting with Xi in Shenzhen, which will be the two leaders’ third get-together this year.

The Treasury secretary has said the two sides are setting up “a direct channel to ensure that either nation can promptly alert the other to serious incidents” related to AI models.

APEC talks could build on the pair’s previous communication channel agreement, Stephen Wu, founder of Carthage Capital, told AFP.

“Both sides need an outcome, and a hotline is diplomacy’s cheapest: free to announce, free to ignore,” he said.

 

First stop: ASEAN summit on Sunday

Trump will attend the ASEAN leaders’ conference in Manila on Sunday before heading to Shenzhen. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Canadian PM Mark Carney are also expected to attend the Southeast Asian talks.

Trade will be a major topic at both ASEAN and APEC, but the prospect of advancing regional free-trade frameworks remains complicated by China-US tensions and Trump’s tariff war.

A pause in the China-US trade war was extended through January 10 during Xi’s September visit to the White House. But friction remains over the level of Chinese rare-earth exports.

For the rest of the APEC and ASEAN nations, no major changes to US trade policy are expected for the time being.

Existing tariff “mechanisms rest with the president and executive branch rather than Congress… reversing them would require legislation the president could veto”, Harry Murphy Cruise, an economist from Oxford Economics, warned in a note.

 

  • Jim Pollard with AFP

data.title: Chinese Exports Soar in October, as Trade Surplus Tops $1 Trillion
data.description:
A big surge in Chinese exports in October caused the country’s trade surplus to top $1 trillion in the first 10 months of 2026, customs data showed on Tuesday.

Exports shot up by 35% year-on-year to $412.3 billion last month, according to the General Administration of Customs, while imports expanded even more, by 41.6% to $307.1 billion.

The country passed the $1 trillion mark even quicker than 2025 and could rise to an all-time high this year, but its industrial ‘overcapacity’ is a sore point in Europe, ASEAN and many other regions around the world, where business people complain that China’s economic policies have had devastating impacts on local industries.

 

ALSO SEE: China Denies Spying on Nvidia CEO, Who Admits Affair, Apologises

 

The figures come ahead of talks between President Xi Jinping and US counterpart Donald Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen next week, when trade tensions will likely loom large.

 

Boom in demand for Chinese AI equipment

Exports from the world’s second-largest economy have shot up in recent months, driven in part by soaring global demand for artificial intelligence-related products, including computer chips, data centre servers and networking equipment.

The trade boom has offered Beijing a key economic lifeline as domestic activity is weighed by longstanding repercussions from the collapse of the once-mighty property sector, which is in the sixth year of a dramatic slump.

That has led to what some economists have called an unbalanced “boom and gloom” domestic economy, as President Xi Jinping has been determined to ramp up military outlays and key tech sectors rather than help middle-class citizens mired in debt because of the property crash.

The figures brought China’s total trade surplus during the first 10 months to a towering $1.04 trillion, according to the GAC.

“Exporters have been the key driving force behind China’s economy this year,” Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, wrote.

“I expect they will continue to perform well in the foreseeable future,” he said, adding that he did not think “China’s macro policy stance will change significantly for the rest of the year”.

The country is well on track to surpass the record $1.2 trillion surplus hit last year, when the $1 trillion mark was reached in November.

However, the export boom continues to fuel tensions with several key trading partners, such as the US and EU, who complain that floods of lower-cost Chinese goods are doing huge damage to local manufacturing.

 

Xi-Trump-Putin summit?

The trade figures will be unwelcome news in Washington, as they showed Chinese exports to the United States surging by a third last month.

They show that the Trump Administration’s tariff strategy – shot down by the US Supreme Court in February – failed to counter the long-running problem of China’s heavy support for key domestic industries and US dependence on rare earth elements sourced from China.

Xi and Trump have navigated a shaky truce to a fierce trade war since their meeting in October last year, agreeing recently to extend the arrangement ahead of talks that were held in Washington in September.

They are expected to hold another head-to-head at the APEC gathering, which runs from November 18 to 19 in Shenzhen and could also see Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin hold trilateral talks.

Last Friday, top Chinese and US officials held what readouts suggested were tetchy talks ahead of the summit.

The Americans stressed “the importance of China fully and immediately implementing its commitments” and highlighted “concerns about recent Chinese actions“, according to the US Treasury Department.

China has been slow to fulfill its promise on a continued supply of rare earths, according to US Trade Rep Jamieson Greer.

But Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng also expressed “serious concerns over recent economic and trade restrictive measures imposed by the United States”, according to a state media report.

 

Brussels also unhappy with trade imbalance

China’s huge trade surplus with the European Union has also rankled Brussels.

Tuesday’s data showed China’s surplus with the 27-nation bloc had swelled to $310.7 billion in January-October – topping the $241.6 billion recorded during the same period last year.

Talks last month in Beijing between EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic and Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao ended with an agreement to limit exports of hybrid vehicles to Europe.

“Trade frictions with the EU have continued to broaden in recent weeks,” wrote Nguyen Hoang Nam of Capital Economics.

Steps taken recently by Brussels to stem the flow of imports, including two-euro fees on all packages entering the bloc, “so far cover only a small portion of China’s exports and are unlikely to have much impact on the economy”, said Nguyen.

Analysts say Beijing is relying heavily on exports to achieve its official growth target for this year of 4.5-5%, its lowest goal in decades.

Domestic consumption has been sluggish for several years, with data on Monday showing inflation was still well short of the official target of around 2%.

 

Australia imposes ‘mandatory’ AI safeguards

Meanwhile, in other Asia-Pacific news, artificial intelligence companies will have to abide by new “mandatory” safeguards when operating in Australia, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday.

Global unease about the power of advanced AI is growing after a string of hacking incidents involving leading companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic.

Australia will establish a new AI safety regulator tasked with implementing measures designed to keep the booming industry in check, Albanese said.

“Our task is to make sure that we shape AI, rather than AI shape us,” Albanese told reporters.

“You can’t turn it off and pretend it isn’t happening. But what we can do is make sure you shape it in Australia’s interest.”

The measures would include “mandatory” reporting of AI security breaches and the independent evaluation of frontier AI models, Albanese said.

“Australia is a first mover in this space and we want to make sure that we reap the potential benefits of AI,” said Albanese.

“But we need to ensure that we get it right, and social licence is absolutely critical.”

Australia voiced deep unease earlier this year after a prototype OpenAI model bypassed safeguards during training and hacked into a government website.

The model sought access to a health statistics portal in June, sidestepping restrictions to breach a section hosting private files.

OpenAI did not raise the alarm with the Australian government until September, when it sent a message to a generic email inbox that is only checked once each day.

Defence minister Richard Marles said AI companies should open themselves to external scrutiny to make sure their tools are safe.

“There needs to be greater risk management of AI capabilities,” he told reporters. “It’s important that there is independent assessment of AI models.”

Marles said it was pointless to pretend that AI would not reshape the world.

“This is not a technology that we can run away from. AI is part of our lives today and it will only grow as part of our lives going forward.”

With immense renewable energy potential and vast stretches of uninhabited land, Australia has billed itself as a prime location for the data centres needed to power artificial intelligence.

OpenAI is involved in the construction of a massive data centre on the outskirts of Sydney.

But AI companies also face a growing local backlash, as many Australians question their ethics and the environmental footprint of their power-hungry data hubs.

A major point of contention is whether Australia will water down its copyright laws so that chatbots can be trained on songs, books and other works of art.

data.title: Hackers in $6bn Hit on Binance Exchange; North Korea Suspected
data.description:
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Friday it was battling to resolve a “complex attack” by hackers that resulted in the theft of about $6.3 billion worth of digital assets.

The company said it coordinated with industry partners, such as stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle, to freeze roughly $3 billion of the stolen funds before they could be laundered or cashed out.

Blockchain intelligence firms such as TRM Labs and Chainalysis have said they believe the attack – the biggest ever to date – was undertaken by TraderTraitor, which is a state-sponsored North Korean hacking unit, reportedly linked to the Lazarus Group.

 

ALSO SEE: Cambodian Regime Seen Deeply Involved in Scam Centres: Amnesty

 

Binance said investigations had “uncovered additional points of breach”, contrary to initial findings that suggested the hack involved a single compromised laptop.

“This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it,” Binance wrote on X.

The firm earlier posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages, insisting that “user funds are completely safe” but also saying it would “cover all losses.”

The company confirmed on its X account for Latin America that “the total estimated impact is around $6.3 billion,” AFP reported.

That is four times the amount impacted in the biggest-ever cyberattack of its kind to date: $1.5 billion taken in February last year from the Bybit platform.

Binance warned the figure “may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets.”

The 2025 Bybit heist was attributed at the time to a group of hackers affiliated with North Korea called TraderTraitor.

Blockchain investigation firm TRM Labs said on Thursday it had “high confidence” that the Binance hack was also orchestrated by TraderTraitor, citing “robust on and off-chain intelligence.”

“Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists,” TRM said.

TraderTraitor is believed to be part of Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for “The Interview,” a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

 

Deposits not affected

At about 0900 GMT Friday, Binance said it was on track to resume withdrawals in 45 hours, after announcing earlier that all deposits and withdrawals had been “temporarily suspended”.

“Deposits remain unaffected,” it said.

The company had said on X that initial investigation suggested the hack involved a compromised laptop belonging to a “DevOps engineer,” allowing the unauthorized party to access a “service container” and execute unauthorized withdrawal transactions.

“We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets,” it said, promising to share a detailed technical analysis once investigations were complete.

But it said later that “subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach.”

Paolo Ardoino, the boss of Tether – a company that issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT – said his firm froze about $1.6 billion “related to a potential Binance exchange hack.”

Jeremy Allaire, who runs cryptocurrency platform Circle, said his company had frozen more than $800 million in USDC.

USDT and USDC are both “stablecoins,” or digital currencies whose value is linked to a traditional currency, the US dollar.

The US Department of Justice and the FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

 

Crypto prices tumble

For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform.

The prices of most major cryptocurrencies fell on news of the cyberattack, except for the stablecoins, which by definition can only fluctuate within tight margins.

Bitcoin and Ethereum plunged nearly 5% and nearly 6%, respectively, on the news. BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10%.

The attack on Binance comes as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

 

  • AFP with additional editing and input by Jim Pollard

data.title: China Denies Spying on Nvidia CEO, Who Admits Affair, Apologises
data.description:
China rejected reports on Monday that it spied on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who admitted to staff on Sunday that he had had an affair.

The issue has become headline news because Huang has developed close ties with US President Donald Trump and US officials allege the woman involved, who is based in Singapore, did work for Chinese intelligence.

Huang sent a note to staff on Sunday admitting the affair after reports that the woman, who works for data-centre company Megaspeed, is also alleged to have ties with China’s Ministry of State Security.

 

ALSO SEE: Asia Markets, Tech Firms Sink on AI Fears; Cyberattacks on Japan

 

That means the issue will be subject to inquiries by not only the board of Nvidia, but likely the new US Congress when it returns under Democrat Party control early next year, analysts have said.

It also affected the group’s share price, which fell by 4% before trading on Monday.

Nvidia’s board announced on Sunday it had opened a probe into chief executive and co-founder Huang after he acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang, a woman who shares the same surname but is not related to the 63-year-old Taiwanese-born tech billionaire.

The New York Times reported late last month that US intelligence officials concluded that Alice Huang, an executive of a data centre company that is a client of Nvidia, had been funnelling information to Beijing.

The executive, also known as Huang Le, developed a close relationship with the Nvidia boss, the Times said.

In a message to company employees released Sunday, the Nvidia chief acknowledged having an affair and apologized to his family and company staff.

“I was unfaithful to my wife,” he said. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Jensen Huang is a huge figure in the artificial intelligence revolution and an informal adviser to President Trump, who has repeatedly spoken out against regulating the industry, so as not to let China gain the upper hand in the AI race.

The Times said Alice Huang’s relationship with the Nvidia chief could have given her insights into Trump’s thinking around AI.

China rejected the spying allegations, with foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun telling a regular briefing on Monday that “the narrative of a so-called Chinese spy is entirely baseless vilification and smearing.”

The issue of AI is likely to arise during Trump’s planned talks with President Xi Jinping later this month at a summit in China.

 

Trump ‘briefed a year ago’

Asked on Sunday whether the Nvidia chief would be joining the president’s trip to Asia, which includes the Asia-Pacific summit in China’s Shenzhen, Trump told reporters: “I don’t know but I’ll certainly take him.”

Trump said Huang was “a fine person, but you never know what’s going on. I’m sure – I hope everything’s fine. He’s done such an incredible job.”

Nvidia said in a statement it had opened an independent probe “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

The statement added: “While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

China is in a race for tech dominance with the United States, which restricts the export to China of the most cutting-edge silicon chips.

Nvidia, a global leader in producing chips used to train and run AI models, is one of the world’s most valuable companies.

Megaspeed was under scrutiny for possibly steering Nvidia AI chips to China, the Times report said, citing unnamed sources briefed on the matter.

Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings about Huang’s relationship with the businesswoman roughly a year ago and chose not to act on the information, the Times report said.

Trump said Sunday he did not regret not acting on this intelligence. “No, I don’t think so. I think – you know, he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.”

 

Scrutiny on sale of chips to China

Technology analyst Dan Ives, with the investment bank Yorkville Ives, said word of the probe is “a black eye moment” for Jensen Huang.

Ives predicted it will at the very least spark multiple congressional inquiries and “create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons.”

In the near-term Jensen Huang is expected to keep his job but risks being removed as Nvidia’s CEO depending on the board’s probe, Ives said in a statement.

“This will also increase major scrutiny regarding selling chips to China, which remains a key battleground issue in DC,” he said.

George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, told AFP that “it would be premature to conclude that Jensen poses a threat to US national security before the facts are fully established.”

“Once you become famous, you will naturally become a target,” Chen said.

“The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised.”

 

  • Jim Pollard with AFP

data.title: Asia Markets, Tech Firms Sink on AI Fears; Cyberattacks on Japan
data.description:
Sharemarkets in Japan and Korea were hit hard on Friday after the plunge on Wall Street overnight, spurred by fears that a Democrat-controlled Congress will ramp up regulation on data centres and the AI sector.

The Nikkei in Tokyo fell by 5.96% and the Kospi in Seoul dropped by 6.02%. The Hang Seng in Hong Kong was down 1.27%, while Shanghai was down 1.1%.

While the historic “blue wave” in mid-term voting on Tuesday was welcomed initially on hopes it could pressure President Donald Trump to wind down his war against Iran, but fears about the impact on the AI buildout soon came to the fore.

 

ALSO SEE: China’s ‘Bipolar’ Economy; Possible 3-Heads Summit in Shenzhen

 

Data centres have faced broad opposition from US voters across the political spectrum, and many midterm winners have pledged to put the brakes on such projects.

Analysts said investors were also spooked by a call from progressive US Senator Bernie Sanders for a national moratorium on their building.

The results compounded already heightened fears about the hundreds of billions firms had pumped into the sector and when they would see a return, while the recent spike in borrowing costs also fuelled concerns about their financial position.

The dramatic rally in many companies’ valuations had also caused unease on trading floors.

Michael Hewson at MCH Market Insights said investors were selling up because of “concerns that we might see greater opposition to AI buildout plans, with the results in Texas prompting concerns that politicians in the state might target Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX due to his support for Trump”.

The Nasdaq in New York plunged 5.5% in its worst day – percentage-wise – since April last year when Trump unveiled his wide-ranging global tariffs. The S&P 500 tanked more than 4% and the Dow more than 3%.

Bloomberg said the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had collapsed around 16% this week, putting it on course for its worst run since April last year.

Trump blamed the collapse on the Democrats, writing on Truth Social: “The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday — So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame!”

 

Kospi down nearly 50% since June

The heavy selling continued in Asia.

Seoul briefly plunged almost 9% before ending 6% lower with chip giant SK Hynix off more than 10% while rival Samsung was 6.4% down.

The Kospi rose by over 75% last year and more than doubled between the end of December and mid-June, when it hit a record, and has lost almost 50% since then.

In Tokyo, SoftBank gave back more than 10%, with Kioxia off 8.7% and Advantest 5% lower.

In Taiwan, TSMC dropped 4.7%, which dragged the Taiex down about the same.

Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Jakarta, Bangkok, Wellington and Manila were also in the red.

Meanwhile, London, Paris and Frankfurt all fell more than 1% when they opened.

Neil Wilson at Saxo Markets said: “The fear is a total momentum unwind as Democrats pace the frontier and kibosh data centre buildout… this looks totally overdone, but the nature of sell-everything of this market means we need to look for some stability first.”

The mood was also dampened by a rise in oil prices, extending Thursday’s gains after plunging on the mid-term results amid hopes for an end to the Iran war.

Traders were keeping eyes on developments in the crisis after US and Iranian leaders had indicated progress earlier in the week.

US jobs data is also due later in the day, following broadly positive readings earlier in the week.

 

Japan responds to cyberattacks

There was plenty of other news in Asia on Friday. First, Japan is set to announce the launch of a “cyber rescue team” later today in response to a sudden wave of hacking incidents.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has vowed to compile an emergency package of measures after dozens of businesses reported unauthorised access in recent weeks to their systems and potential leaks of client data.

Hacks and data breaches have ballooned worldwide, with AI’s ability to find previously unknown ways to break into computer systems in the global spotlight.

Takaichi’s office confirmed her cabinet will hold a ministerial meeting on cybersecurity on Friday.

The policy package will include the creation of a “cyber rescue team” made up of both government and private sector experts, the Yomiuri Shimbun daily, Jiji Press and other media reported.

The government will set up a secretariat within the current fiscal year to coordinate the deployment of the rescue team when support needs are particularly acute, the reports said.

A “Top Gun Talent Team” of specialists will also be deployed this month to simulate attacks in a push to boost security, Jiji Press reported.

The measures will be “the first step towards transitioning to a society that meets the world’s top standards of cyber resilience”, top government spokesman Minoru Kihara told reporters on Thursday.

The package will be “one that prevents damage from occurring as much as possible, and, if damage does occur, is able to respond immediately”, he said.

Chinese artificial intelligence cybersecurity tool Artex was used in several recent hacks of Japanese companies, an information security arm of Japanese IT firm GMO Internet Group said last month. GMO Internet Group is among those that have come under attack.

 

Protest over Moscow seizing Japan Tobacco assets

Meanwhile, Tokyo lodged a protest with Moscow demanding the immediate release of Japan Tobacco’s assets that were seized by the Kremlin, government spokesman Minoru Kihara said on Friday.

Kihara said two Japanese senior officials visiting Russia “had lodged a protest with the Russian government together with the ambassador of Japan to Russia, and demanded the immediate withdrawal of the measure”.

data.title: China’s ‘Bipolar’ Economy; Possible 3-Heads Summit in Shenzhen
data.description:
A former senior official at the IMF noted last week that China appears to have an extraordinary ‘boom and gloom’ economy – a country with two very different sides.

Kenneth Rogoff, a former chief economist at the International Monetary Fund, said that while China’s export industries such as EVs, solar panels and many manufactured goods are “the envy of the world”, the country’s growth is “deeply unbalanced.”

While its tech and AI industries are topped only by the United States, the rest of its economy is stuck in the sixth year of a “full-blown, Japan-style real estate crisis,” which has left domestic consumption stagnating in the doldrums.

 

ALSO SEE: Chinese Stocks Rise; Dollar Down on Democrats’ Electoral Sweep

 

Part of the country’s problem is that its dynamic sectors, such as robotics and AI, are not creating enough jobs, which means the country’s youth unemployment problem is so bad that Beijing no longer publishes the figures regularly.

Because China is not a democracy, it is possible, he said, that 450 million people are part of the most dynamic sectors that are currently thriving, while more than double that number – another 950 million citizens – have to survive on a “much lower” standard of living, despite the fact President Xi’s regime has sought to ease regional disparities since he came to power in 2013.

Wealth inequality is a problem that plagues countries all over the world, including America.

Rogoff, a former professor of economics and public policy at Harvard and an author of multiple books, who is 73 now, said that China’s excessive construction is likely to “hold down growth for years to come.”

But he suggested the dynamic core of its industrial sector should continue to thrive, as long as it remains politically stable – and doesn’t fall for “temptations of imperial overreach.”

There was no mention of Taiwan. All the indicators and reports we’ve seen in recent years suggest Rogoff is right on the money. His latest report can be read here.

 

Three leaders to meet?

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump appears to have taken the battering endured by his Republican allies in the mid-term elections this week in relatively subdued fashion.

Washington is alive with speculation on how the ‘blue wave’ that has dramatically changed the country’s political scene will play out.

Beijing is still eager to lure the US leader to the APEC summit it will hold in Shenzhen this month – and it’s possible that Trump has bigger things in mind than his party’s electoral drubbing.

China said on Wednesday it was in contact with the United States and Russia about a possible three-way leaders’ meeting on the sidelines of the regional gathering in Shenzhen in a couple of weeks time.

“China is in communication on a China-Russia-US heads of state meeting with relevant parties,” foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told a regular briefing when asked about the possible trilateral summit on the sidelines of the APEC meeting on November 18-19, AFP reported.

The Kremlin said on October 21 that the meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US and Russian counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin – which would be a first – was “being prepared”.

Xi, 73, and Trump, 80, have already met twice this year – most recently with the Chinese leader visiting the White House in September – and they are due to come together again at a G20 summit in Miami in December.

The two leaders vowed to extend a trade truce they agreed in October 2025 and to explore tariff cuts on $30 billion of goods on each side.

 

Denuclearization, end to Ukraine war?

Trump last met Putin, 74, in person in Alaska in August 2025. And the US leader said last month he wanted to hold a trilateral summit with Putin and Xi in China to discuss “denuclearization.”

He told reporters at the White House on October 20 that a three-way summit would be “a very positive thing for the world.”

Putin is alleged to have suggested the idea to Trump in a phone call on October 9, perhaps to broker an end to the war in Ukraine, without having Ukraine present for initial talks, according to sources that spoke to the Wall Street Journal.

Xi and Putin have, of course, met many times, including in May when the Russian leader visited Beijing.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned last month that a trilateral summit could offer a platform to redistribute influence, similar to after World War II.

“We really don’t want this to turn into ‘Yalta 2, 3, 4’, with a redistribution of influence,” he said, referring to the 1945 summit of Soviet, US and British leaders on dividing up the post-war map.

“Russia wants this meeting more than anyone,” Zelensky said, warning against handing Moscow “another major diplomatic advantage”.

 

Ukraine honour for Melania

But US officials have just announced that US First Lady Melania Trump will host officials from Moscow and Kyiv at the White House on Thursday, ahead of talks in Abu Dhabi aimed at ending the Ukraine war.

The talks have revived hopes for peace, as Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine grinds through its fifth year, and a recent rapprochement between Trump and Putin has raised concerns the US could turn its back on Kyiv.

Moscow’s adviser for international economic cooperation, Kirill Dmitriev, and human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova plan to meet Melania Trump on Thursday “provided that all logistical arrangements work out”, Russia’s state-owned TASS news agency reported on Wednesday, citing Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, announced he would also be meeting Melania Trump in Washington.

The meeting comes after Zelensky said he had “very detailed, hour-and-a-half-long” conversations with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner ahead of next week’s meeting in Abu Dhabi, the first talks between all three sides since February.

Earlier on Wednesday, Zelensky awarded the first lady a national honour for her role in brokering a partial ceasefire that allowed the evacuation of civilians from a Russian-occupied town.

The text acknowledged her “significant personal contribution to humanitarian support for Ukraine, and for active human rights and charitable work.”

Melania, who is expected to speak at 11am (1600 GMT) on Thursday, had announced a localized truce between Ukrainian and Russian forces last month to allow for residents of Oleshky on the southern front to leave after suffering weeks of shortages of food and medicine.

The rare halt in fighting, which was respected by both sides, allowed roads to be demined and residents to depart for either Ukraine or Russia.

She has also been involved in efforts to return Ukrainian children taken to Russia.

 

  • Jim Pollard with AFP

data.title: Chinese Stocks Rise; Dollar Down on Democrats’ Electoral Sweep
data.description:
The Chinese government’s intervention to rescue local stocks hammered by a prolonged ‘tech slump’ finally began to restore share values in Shanghai on Wednesday.

A $15-billion “barrage” of moves announced by the People’s Bank of China and financial regulators on Monday helped lift the CSI 300 index in Shanghai by up to 2%, although the gains were attributed to “state-backed investors,” according to the South China Morning Post.

Retail investors, it said, “refrained from bets on stocks this week, even after Beijing unveiled a litany of measures to shore up confidence in the world’s second-largest equity market.”

 

ALSO SEE: China Unveils Measures to Boost Markets after Big Falls in October

 

“Leveraged traders trimmed their holdings to a one-year low this week, while new stock-account openings dropped by more than 30% in October, according to official data.

“The retreat in retail enthusiasm contrasted with the government ramping up its efforts to prop up stocks, including liquidity injections through two monetary tools and reported suspensions of new share sales to keep a lid on supply,” the paper said this afternoon.

“There is a difference between stopping the bleeding and restoring the patient to full health,” it quoted Stephen Innes, a managing partner at SPI Asset Management, as saying.

“State-backed buying can steady the tape. Easier buy-back financing can improve liquidity. But if corporate earnings do not improve, the market eventually comes back to the same question. Who is buying once the government steps away?”

The CSI index had fallen for 12 consecutive weeks and stocks on China’s mainland had lost about $2.4 trillion in market value since May because investors had lost faith that Beijing’s AI boom would ever make a profit.

 

Study: Less disclosure to foreign investors

Another possible reason for the slump was a study published in The Accounting Review, which found that Chinese companies frequently provide less complete information to foreign investors than to domestic shareholders.

It said that English-language filings systematically offered less comprehensive information than their domestic Chinese counterparts, and that when researchers emailed Chinese companies posing as local versus foreign investors, the firms were half as likely to respond to the foreign inquiries.

The response gap worsened for companies with larger translation disparities in their public reports, according to the Wall Street Journal’s China correspondent.

Even native-Mandarin-speaking analysts at foreign brokerages suffered from a lack of direct communication, leading to less accurate earnings forecasts, the WSJ said, noting that selective disclosure reduces stock liquidity, and makes it harder and more expensive for these firms to raise capital.

 

Democratic sweep in US

Meanwhile, the big news of the day was the Democrat Party’s sweep of both Congress and the US Senate in the mid-term elections on Tuesday, which looks set to derail Donald Trump’s economic agenda as he heads into his final two years as president.

Equities and the dollar sank initially amid warnings that the result – which saw Republicans ousted in a so-called blue wave – could lead to gridlock on Capitol Hill after Trump warned that he would become “Mr Veto”.

Tech firms, already under pressure, were also hit by concerns about the future of data centre building – a major bone of contention in many places.

Tens of millions of Americans cast their vote in the crucial polls pitched as a referendum on the White House amid anger at surging petrol prices, tariffs and the Iran war.

With Democrats winning key races to flip the House and Senate – including once-safe Republican seats – Chris Weston at Pepperstone flagged “the potential for legislative gridlock, fiscal brinkmanship, debt-ceiling disputes, and congressional investigations,” AFP reported.

However, he added that “the president would retain considerable executive authority, so the implications for individual sectors are far from straightforward”.

Trump threatened in a telephone interview with the CBS network on Tuesday to be “Mr Veto” and block any Democratic legislation if they win.

The prospect of Congress coming to a standstill weighed on the dollar and Treasury yields, with observers pointing out that such a scenario would restrict spending.

Gold rose 2% after the vote, while cryptocurrencies dipped briefly amid concern over greater regulation on digital assets.

Bitcoin briefly hit a six-week low before recovering to trade close to flat by 0715 GMT at $78,070. Analysts say support has also been hit by the $6-billion hack of the Binance exchange late last week, which is the largest-ever crypto heist.

 

‘Poll could cut inflation, Treasury yields’

“Democratic control of Congress will make it harder for the White House administration to pass major partisan legislation. That could reduce the prospect of significant additional fiscal stimulus over the next two years,” wrote David Chao at Invesco.

“For Asia, the implications matter. Less fiscal stimulus could reduce upward pressure on US growth, inflation and Treasury yields, potentially easing some of the pressure that higher US rates and a stronger dollar have placed on Asian currencies and monetary policy.”

However, as the results came in, he offered a more conciliatory tone to the New York Times, saying he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” and expected to work out deals with Democrats.

That provided the queue for a bounce in some stock markets, as well as the dollar and Treasury yields.

Hong Kong, Shanghai, Seoul and reversed losses, while Mumbai, Bangkok, Wellington and Manila were also up.

However, Tokyo, Sydney, Taipei and Jakarta all fell.

London, Paris and Frankfurt opened with gains.

 

Doubt over AI buildout

While they managed to pare losses, tech firms remained under pressure as investors continue to fret over the AI investment boom and when firms that have pumped billions into the sector will eventually see returns, if ever.

Traders were also nervous about the outlook for the AI buildout, with many Democrats taking advantage of anger over data centre development.

“The concern isn’t that a Democratic governor automatically shuts the gates on data-centre construction,” said Stephen Innes at SPI Asset Management.

“It is that a change in political leadership could alter the regulatory environment just as developers are committing enormous amounts of capital to projects dependent on electricity availability and predictable construction schedules.”

However, Google was happy to announce plans on Wednesday to invest $15 billion in Malaysia over the next two years to build data centres and other digital infrastructure as demand for AI services booms in Asia.

The US tech giant said its data centre campuses in industrial zones would be “energy-efficient” while pledging to “bolster local water security, and add more than one gigawatt of clean energy capacity” to Malaysia’s national grid.

 

Tech stocks slide, Iran says ‘no to war’

Meanwhile, Japanese chipmaker Kioxia plunged more than 5%, while Advantest and SoftBank lost more than 3%. Seoul’s SK Hynix and Samsung were also down.

Oil prices edged up as investors kept tabs on the Middle East after Trump confirmed US strikes on Iran but played down speculation he was preparing to resume bombing after the election.

“We seem to be getting everything we want,” he told the Financial Times newspaper on Tuesday.

“I’m ready, we’re ready. We’re locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it.”

His Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian said his government was trying to resolve the crisis “through dialogue”, adding that “no one will benefit from this war” if it reignited.

However, Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Islamic republic was “ready for battle with its finger on the trigger”, while Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Tehran retained the right to “legitimate self-defence”.

He later posted on X that “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message”.

data.title: China Unveils Measures to Boost Markets after Big Falls in October
data.description:
Authorities in China announced a range of measures on Monday to bolster local equity markets, which suffered severe declines in October.

The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) unveiled a 100-billion-yuan ($15 billion) asset swap facility with 31 securities firms, plus asset management companies and insurers. That is a one-year arrangement which is due to start on Tuesday.

The central bank also said it would increase the number of institutions that can participate in the scheme and introduce a small cut to reduce swap fees.

 

ALSO SEE: Cambodian Regime Seen Deeply Involved in Scam Centres: Amnesty

 

The central bank will reduce the interest rate – from 1.25% to 1% – on a special relending program to support share buybacks and help major shareholders increase equity stakes, it said.

It has urged commercial banks to scale up lending and said the policy to do that will be permanent, the South China Morning Post said.

Officials with the PBOC met with their counterparts from the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) and other regulators today in a bid to stabilize local markets and show they would defend equity markets after the sell-off last month that rocked investors.

Institutional investors will be able to trade illiquid assets with the central bank to be able to buy stocks, the paper said.

Meanwhile, the CSRC plans to expand the scope of relending and support tools to encourage more tech companies to participate and attract major index constituents.

Regulators will also ease restrictions on leveraged trading and indicated that state-linked investors, often known as the “national team”, which help counter sell-offs in tech and AI-related equities.

The CSI 300 index, which tracks the largest companies in Shanghai and Shenzhen, slumped by 8.5% last month. It became a bear market on October 20, after a 20% drop, and had fallen for 12 consecutive weeks.

The Star 50 index in Shanghai, dominated by large chip and tech firms, has been one of the worst hit. It has plunged by about 40% in less than four months, and seen share losses of about $480 billion.

Stocks on China’s mainland have lost about $2.4 trillion in market value since May, according to Yahoo Finance, which said last week that investors had lost faith that Beijing’s AI boom would ever make a profit.

Goldman Sachs says AI companies have about 42% of the market value of Chinese shares listed on the mainland and in Hong Kong, over half of current of trading, which means when they fall, they drag the local markets down with them.

The main problem appears to be doubt that AI companies and other tech firms, such as those making robots, will ever earn back the money spent on their products.

News of Beijing’s intent to support local markets helped lift Shanghai by 1.08% on Monday, while the Hang Seng in Hong Kong was also up 0.42%.

 

Oil prices fall

Meanwhile, in other business news, oil prices fell about 6% on Monday because of the flurry of talks going on to try to end the war in the Middle East. Brent crude was just over $106 a barrel, while WTI was at $97.45.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that “very intensive” talks are underway with the United States via mediators, amid fears that the war might reignite after the US mid-term elections this week.

“Given the sensitivity and gravity of the current situation, consultations and deliberations are very intensive. Qatar and Pakistan are playing a very active mediating role in these negotiations,” he said in a video interview given to the official IRNA news agency.

China stepped up diplomatic efforts on Monday to resolve the Middle East crisis, urging a return to the negotiating table in back-to-back meetings with Iranian, Omani and Saudi officials in Beijing.

The meetings come days after US President Donald Trump issued a fresh war threat more than eight months into the conflict, which was triggered by US-Israeli strikes on Iran and has at times spilled over into neighbouring countries.

Beijing supports Tehran in “safeguarding its own sovereignty and security”, Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Ali Bagheri Kani, the deputy secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, according to a Chinese statement.

Wang later called for dialogue to end the conflict “while safeguarding regional energy security and the safety of shipping lanes”, as he met with Saudi National Security Adviser Musaad bin Mohammad al-Aiban.

China, a top economic partner of Iran, has long sought a detente in the months-long conflict that has disrupted global shipping.

Trump said on Saturday that the United States had knocked out much of Iran’s military but still has to “take care of” one or two targets, with Tehran warning of reprisals if attacked.

“All parties should… in a spirit of reason and pragmatism, focus on a political solution rather than once again resorting to armed conflict,” Wang told Bagheri Kani, according to the statement.

 

  • Jim Pollard with AFP
